questions.q: Decompose turns the task-tracker spec into 15 components across 3 waves: Wave 0 holds the 4 entity models and 2 configs, Wave 1 holds CacheService and AuthService, Wave 2 holds AuthMiddleware and the 6 handlers. What determines which wave a given component lands in?
options: Its estimated complexity — cheap, low-complexity components are scheduled into earlier waves so each wave finishes fast.
Its channel source — data-model components always precede API components regardless of what actually depends on what.
The depth of its dependency chain: a component lands in the first wave by which every component it depends on has already been built.
The alphabetical order of its component id, so a given spec always decomposes identically.
questions.explanation: Waves come out of a topological sort over the dependency graph: each wave is the set of components whose dependencies were all satisfied by an earlier wave. Complexity feeds the time *estimate*, never the placement. Channel source drives the wave's human-readable label — the handlers sit in Wave 2 not because they are 'API work' but because they depend on AuthService, which depends on Wave 0's configs. And ordering *within* a wave is meaningless by construction, since everything in a wave runs at the same time, so an alphabetical rule would have nothing to sort.

questions.q: The build package header reads `15 components · 3 waves · 7× parallelism`. Wave 0 has 6 components, Wave 1 has 2, Wave 2 has 7. Where does the `7×` come from, and what consumes it?
options: 15 ÷ 3 — components divided by waves — and the Build Agent uses it to decide how many waves to run at once.
The size of the largest wave; the Build Agent reads it from the package metadata and uses it as the thread-pool worker cap for every wave.
The number of distinct component types in the plan; it is a reporting metric the Build Agent ignores.
15 − (3 × 2): the count of components that have no dependencies at all.
questions.explanation: Max parallelism is the width of the widest wave — here Wave 2's 7 components. It is demonstrably not an average: 15 ÷ 3 = 5, which is not the number printed. The Build Agent lifts `max_parallelism` straight out of the build package's metadata and hands it to its thread pool as the worker count, so the pool is sized once for the worst case and reused; narrower waves just leave workers idle. Waves are never run concurrently with each other — Wave N+1's inputs literally do not exist until Wave N has finished — so there is nothing for a 'how many waves at once' knob to control.

questions.q: Decompose reports `73% time savings` for the 15-component, 3-wave plan. A learner computes (15 − 3) ÷ 15 = 80% and asks why the tool disagrees with them. What is the tool actually computing?
options: It caps the reported figure at 73% to stay deliberately conservative.
It subtracts measured LLM latency and network overhead from the ideal figure.
It divides the number of dependency edges by the number of components.
It compares complexity-weighted minutes: sequential time sums every component's own estimate, parallel time sums only the slowest component in each wave.
questions.explanation: Savings = (sequential − parallel) ÷ sequential, where every component contributes a fixed estimate by complexity band (low 10 min, medium 20, high 30). Sequential adds up all 15 components; parallel adds up just the slowest member of each wave, because a wave takes as long as its longest component. The learner's (components − waves) ÷ components shortcut only coincides with the real number when every component sits in the same complexity band — mixed complexity is exactly why 80% and 73% diverge. Nothing is capped, and no measured runtime enters the number: this is a static estimate produced at decompose time, before a single LLM call has been made.

questions.q: Part 3 of the build package lists interface contracts such as `IAuthService`, each with an explicit `Owner: AuthService` line and a `Types: AuthCredentials, AuthToken, TokenPayload` line. Why is ownership pinned before any code is generated?
options: Exactly one component implements the interface; every other component is told to import it and NOT implement it, so two components generated in the same wave cannot emit competing definitions of the same contract.
So the Deploy Agent knows which container should receive traffic for that interface.
So the ~500-line build package can be sorted by owner and is easier for a human to read.
Because the generating model refuses to emit a component whose interface has no named owner.
questions.explanation: Parallel generation is only safe if the shared boundary is settled first. AuthMiddleware's build prompt says `Depends on (import, do not implement): IAuthService` — the Owner field is what makes that instruction unambiguous about who does implement it. Without a single named owner, two components generated concurrently by independent LLM calls would each invent their own `AuthToken` shape and the assembled project would not compile. Ownership is a build-time consistency guarantee; it has no runtime meaning, so routing is irrelevant, and readability is a side effect rather than the reason.

questions.q: Part 4 of the build package is `Component Build Prompts` — one prompt per component, 15 of them for this MVP. What does a single component's prompt contain?
options: The entire dense spec, so the model generating that component has the full architectural picture.
Just the component name — the Build Agent looks up everything else at build time.
The component's role, only the spec constraints that apply to it, the interface it must implement with method signatures, and the interfaces it must import but not implement.
The component's prompt plus the expected file contents, so the model can diff its output against the target.
questions.explanation: Each prompt is a deliberately narrow slice. AuthService's prompt carries its purpose, the three auth constraints that actually bear on it (RS256 signing, RBAC roles owner/admin/member, 15m access + 30d refresh), its `Must implement: IAuthService` method signatures, and its import-only dependencies. The full dense spec is Part 1 of the package for human and orchestrator reference — it is *not* what each per-component call receives, because handing every component the whole spec recreates the exact failure decomposition exists to prevent. The Build Agent does add mechanical detail later (target path, runtime, allowed packages), but the component's purpose and constraints travel in the prompt, and there is no reference implementation to diff against — the file does not exist yet.

questions.q: The Build Agent's Wrap Prompt stage wraps the decompose-supplied component prompt before it reaches the LLM. What does the wrapper add?
options: The target file path, the runtime version, the list of packages already installed in the image, and a file-shape template for that component type and language.
The full dense spec, the wave plan, the dependency graph, and every interface contract.
A system prompt, a temperature, a token budget, and a stop sequence.
The Dockerfile, package.json and .env.example, so the model can see the project layout.
questions.explanation: The wrapper exists to make the output *mechanically usable*, not to add architectural context. It names the exact target file (`src/auth-service.js`), pins the runtime (Node 20), enumerates the packages actually installed in the image so the model cannot import something that will not resolve, and pastes a shape template for that component type and language so the emitted file matches project conventions. It also opens with `Output the file CONTENTS ONLY — no markdown fences, no prose` — a formatting instruction inside the prompt text, not a sampling parameter. Re-injecting the whole spec would undo decomposition; the Dockerfile and dependency manifest do not exist yet at this stage, since Assemble writes them after the components are generated.

questions.q: A build has two waves: Wave 0 (weather-service, health-handler) and Wave 1 (weather-handler, app-server). How many LLM calls does the Build Agent make, and in what pattern?
options: One call for the whole build — the model emits all four files in a single response.
Two calls, one per wave, each returning that wave's files together.
Four calls, all four dispatched concurrently, with a reconciliation pass afterwards to fix ordering problems.
Four calls, one per component: Wave 0's two dispatched concurrently, then — only once both have returned — Wave 1's two dispatched concurrently.
questions.explanation: One LLM call per component is the unit of isolation: each call sees only its own component's prompt, which is what keeps a bad generation contained to a single file instead of corrupting the whole project. Within a wave the calls are submitted to a thread pool and run at the same time, so the wave's wall clock is roughly its slowest component rather than the sum — that is where the 32.9s total for 4 components comes from. Between waves the agent blocks until every call in the wave has resolved, because Wave 1's components were placed there precisely because they depend on Wave 0's output. Firing all four at once would discard the ordering the wave plan exists to enforce, and no post-hoc pass can recover a dependency that was not available when the code was written.

questions.q: The Python Dockerfile the Build Agent writes ends with `CMD ["python", "src/app.py"]`, but a decompose-derived build package usually contains no `app` component. What does the Assemble stage do about that?
options: It rewrites the Dockerfile's CMD to point at whichever generated file looks most like an entrypoint.

It writes an `src/app.py` shim — only if the build did not already generate one — that creates the Flask app, auto-registers every module-level Blueprint found in sibling `src/*.py` files, and always serves `/healthz`.
It fails the build and tells the user to add an `app` component to the build package.
It concatenates every generated Python file into one `src/app.py` so the CMD resolves.
questions.explanation: The generated components are Flask *fragments* — a `Blueprint(...)` plus `@bp.get(...)` handlers — with no `Flask(__name__)` and no `app.run()`. With a fixed CMD and no `src/app.py`, the container dies on start with `can't open file '/app/src/app.py'`. The shim supplies the missing assembly layer without editing a single generated file, and the existence check means a build that genuinely produced its own entrypoint keeps it rather than being overwritten. The always-on `/healthz` is not decoration: it guarantees the Kubernetes probe has something to hit even when no generated handler exposed a health route. Concatenating files would collide on imports and duplicate route registrations; rewriting the CMD per build would make the image's start command unpredictable.

questions.q: For one component, the LLM returns the text "I cannot generate this file without more information about your database schema." What does the Build Agent do?
options: Writes the text to the target source file anyway; the Docker build will catch it later.
Retries the same prompt until code comes back.
Raises a post-process error, writes no file for that component, and lets the rest of the wave finish.
Substitutes a stub that satisfies the component's interface so the build stays green.
questions.explanation: Post-processing is a validity gate, not a formatter. If the response is fenced, the first fenced block is extracted; if it is unfenced, the first non-blank line must begin with a code-like token (`import`, `from`, `def`, `class`, `const`, `export`, and so on). Prose fails both tests, so the agent raises a post-process error and no file is written — deferring the failure to the Docker build would turn a clear per-component error into a confusing syntax error. The failure is scoped to that one component: it is emitted as an error event while the other components in the wave still complete, which is the concrete payoff of one call per component. Note what does *not* happen — no automatic retry and no stub substitution. Recovering a failed component is a human decision in this pipeline.

questions.q: A JavaScript build of 4 components finishes. Which files exist in that run's workspace folder?
options: Only the 4 generated `src/*.js` files — packaging is the Deploy Agent's job.
The 4 generated `src/*.js` files plus a `Dockerfile`, a `package.json`, a `.env.example`, and an `src/app-server.js` entrypoint if none was generated.
The 4 generated files plus a Helm chart and a Kubernetes Deployment manifest.
The 4 generated files plus a test suite and a CI workflow.
questions.explanation: Assemble writes the project-level files the generated sources cannot produce for themselves: a language-appropriate Dockerfile (`node:20-alpine`, `EXPOSE 3000`, `CMD ["node","src/app-server.js"]`), a dependency manifest listing exactly the packages the prompt told the model it was allowed to use (`package.json` for JavaScript, `requirements.txt` for Python), a `.env.example` naming the secrets a developer still has to supply, and the entrypoint shim when the build did not generate one. Kubernetes YAML is rendered later by the Deploy Agent from a template, against the workspace — it is not a build artefact. Tests and CI workflows are never emitted anywhere in this pipeline; that is Module 5's subject.

questions.q: The Deploy Agent auto-derives `healthcheck_path` from the built workspace rather than accepting a default. How does it choose, and what happens if it finds nothing?
options: It defaults to `/`, so rendering always succeeds.
It reads the path out of the dense spec's Deployment section.
It starts the container locally and records whichever path returns 200.

It scans the generated sources for GET route literals and takes the first hit from a fixed priority list (`/healthz`, `/health`, `/readyz`, `/ready`, `/ping`, `/`); if no routes are found at all it refuses to render rather than defaulting.
questions.explanation: Rendering YAML with a *guessed* health path is worse than failing loudly, because Kubernetes will then mark a perfectly healthy pod unready and the mistake resurfaces minutes later as a rollout that never completes. So an empty `healthcheck_path` is treated as a hard error at render time. The derivation is a static scan of the generated sources for GET route registrations, resolved against a fixed preference order and falling back to the shortest discovered route only when none of the preferred paths exist. It cannot probe a container — nothing is running yet when the YAML is rendered — and the spec's Deployment section describes hosting, not routes. This is also why the entrypoint shim registers `/healthz`: it makes the scan succeed by construction.

questions.q: Two different apps are built and deployed through the pipeline. What do they share in ECR, and what keeps them from colliding?
options: Both push to the same `architect-builds/app` repository; only the image tag is per-run unique, and nothing collides because the Kubernetes Application name and ingress host are still derived from the spec slug plus run id.
Nothing is shared — each app gets its own ECR repository named after its spec slug.
They share a repository and a tag; the newer push simply overwrites the older image.
They share a repository and a tag, and the Kubernetes Application name is randomly generated to keep them apart.
questions.explanation: The registry path is deliberately decoupled from the spec slug. One shared repository means the ECR repo-creation pre-flight happens once ever instead of once per new app, and is a no-op on every subsequent build. Uniqueness lives in two other places: the image tag carries the short run id (`...:d9331c`, so images never overwrite each other), and the Kubernetes object name plus ingress host carry the app identity (`quote-of-the-day-d9331c`, `quote-of-the-day-d9331c-training.tools.fubotv.net`). Random names would give you uniqueness without identity — you could no longer tell which running Application corresponds to which app.

questions.q: The Deploy Agent always builds with `docker build --platform linux/amd64`. If that flag were dropped and the build ran on an Apple Silicon laptop, what would fail, and when?
options: `docker build` would fail immediately with an unsupported-architecture error.
`docker push` would be rejected by ECR for an architecture mismatch.
Build and push would both succeed; the pod would then sit in ImagePullBackOff on the cluster with `no match for platform in manifest`.
Nothing would fail — the kubelet emulates the mismatched architecture transparently.
questions.explanation: This is a late-binding failure, which is exactly why the flag is pinned instead of left to the host default. Docker on an arm64 machine happily builds an arm64 image, and ECR is a content-agnostic registry that happily stores it — neither step has any reason to object. The mismatch is only discovered when an amd64 node's kubelet tries to pull the image and finds no matching platform in the manifest, at which point you are debugging a crash-looping pod two green steps and several minutes downstream of the actual cause. Pinning `--platform` moves the decision to the only place that knows the deployment target: the build.

questions.q: You apply a manifest in which only the image tag changed (`abc123` → `def456`); replicas stay at 2. What does the cluster actually do?
options: The API server patches the two running containers in place with the new image.

The Deployment controller diffs desired against actual state, creates a NEW ReplicaSet for `def456`, and the default rolling update (maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0) brings up a replacement and waits for its readiness probe before terminating an old pod.
Both running pods are deleted, then two fresh pods are created from the new image.
`kubectl apply` blocks until every pod is Ready and then returns; nothing happens asynchronously.
questions.explanation: A pod's image cannot be edited in place, so a tag change can only be realised by creating new pods — which is why a second ReplicaSet appears and the old one is scaled to zero rather than mutated. The rolling-update defaults are what make the swap zero-downtime: maxUnavailable 0 forbids killing an old pod before its replacement reports Ready, maxSurge 1 allows exactly one extra pod during the overlap, and the Service selector routes only to Ready pods so traffic never lands on a starting container. Deleting both pods first would be a hard outage. And `apply` is asynchronous — it returns as soon as the API server has stored the desired state; observing the rollout is a separate `kubectl rollout status` call.

questions.q: A pipeline run ends with a live URL returning HTTP 200. What has the pipeline verified?
options: Only that the ingress served a successful response at the derived health path — nothing about behavioural correctness, and no tests ran at any point in the pipeline.
That the generated code passes its tests and that the deploy config validated cleanly.
That the app is correct, since a 200 from the health path exercises the generated handlers.
That the rollout is being monitored and will roll back automatically if it degrades.
questions.explanation: The only assertion the pipeline makes is transport-level: it polls the ingress every 5 seconds for up to 120 seconds and stops at the first 200 or 302. No automated tests run as part of the build, there is no deploy-config validation, no health-monitoring dashboard, and no rollback or blue-green strategy — every one of those is Module 5. Module 4's own live run makes the gap concrete: the deployed app returned a genuine 200 while its `/quote` handler was a functional stub returning `{"result":"value"}`. A green pipeline means 'running and reachable', not 'working'.
